strengths: Clean and simple theoretical derivation showing SFT gradient is equivalent to a policy gradient with an implicit inverse-probability-weighted reward, providing a novel and intuitive explanation for SFT's poor generalization compared to RL.
The proposed fix (DFT) is extremely simple to implement (a one-line reweighting of the loss by the stop-gradient token probability), making it easy to adopt and reproduce.

Extensive empirical validation across five model families/sizes (LLaMA-3.2-3B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, DeepSeekMath-7B, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B) and five challenging math benchmarks, showing consistent and often large improvements over standard SFT.

Comparison against a concurrent and closely related method (iw-SFT) as well as offline/online RL baselines (DPO, RFT, PPO, GRPO), showing DFT is competitive or superior while being computationally simpler (no reference model needed).

Useful ablations on learning rate and batch size sensitivity, and an interesting qualitative analysis of token probability distributions (bimodal effect) that offers some mechanistic insight into why DFT works.
Interesting connection/contrast drawn to Focal Loss, highlighting a conceptually opposite reweighting philosophy relevant to the LLM overfitting regime.
weaknesses: The derivation in Eq. 5 treats the expert distribution as a Dirac delta and introduces an importance weight 1/π_θ(y|x) over full sequences; converting this to a per-token version in Eq. 9 is done heuristically ("a common treatment" borrowed from PPO) without rigorous justification that the token-level rescaling preserves the intended reward-rectification property or remains an unbiased/consistent estimator of any well-defined objective. The theoretical soundness of the final practical loss is thus weaker than the paper's rhetoric suggests.

The reward r(x,y)=1[y=y*] used to derive Eq. 6 is only nonzero on a measure-zero set for continuous/discrete sequence spaces, making the "policy gradient" interpretation somewhat degenerate/formal rather than a rigorous RL equivalence; the paper does not discuss convergence, bias, or consistency properties of the resulting DFT estimator under this reinterpretation.

Evaluation is limited entirely to mathematical reasoning tasks; despite claims of "multiple challenging benchmarks," all benchmarks are variants of math reasoning (Math500, Minerva, OlympiadBench, AIME, AMC) drawn from largely overlapping distributions to the training data (NuminaMath), so generalization claims to broader domains (code, instruction following, general QA) are unsupported — acknowledged as a limitation but this substantially limits the paper's claimed significance.
No experiments with larger models (>7B) or with modern instruction-tuned/non-math base models, despite the framing of the contribution as a general improvement to SFT for LLMs broadly.

Single-run results are implied (no variance/error bars reported across seeds) for the main table, despite the averaging over 16 decoding samples per model; given the sometimes large swings (e.g., AIME24 numbers based on very few problems), statistical significance of differences is unclear, especially in Table 2/3 where DFT loses to iw-SFT or GRPO on some individual benchmarks.

The explanation of the bimodal token-probability phenomenon (Section 4.3.1) is descriptive and speculative ("akin to human pedagogy") rather than analytically grounded; no quantitative link is established between this phenomenon and the observed generalization gains.

Limited novelty relative to concurrent/contemporaneous work (iw-SFT, Wang et al. 2025, Qin & Springenberg 2025) that already frames SFT within an RL/importance-weighting perspective; the paper's differentiation (exact 1/π cancellation vs. more general importance weighting) is real but somewhat incremental in conceptual scope, even though the empirical results are stronger.

The RL/offline-RL section (4.2) is labeled 'exploratory' and uses a single model (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B) and a single training set scale, which is insufficient to strongly support the claim that DFT is broadly competitive with or superior to established online RL methods like GRPO/PPO.
Missing details on variance across training seeds, and no code/artifact yet released (stated as "will be available"), somewhat limiting immediate reproducibility during review.

strengths: The core idea (reweighting the SFT loss by stop-gradient token probability) is extremely simple to implement and the paper provides an intuitive derivation connecting the SFT gradient to a policy-gradient form, which is a nice pedagogical framing even if not fully novel.

The empirical evaluation spans multiple model families and sizes (LLaMA-3.2-3B/3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B, DeepSeekMath-7B) and consistently shows DFT improving over vanilla SFT, including on harder benchmarks where SFT degrades performance (Olympiad Bench, AIME24, AMC23).

The paper includes a reasonably thorough set of ablations (learning rate, batch size) and an interesting qualitative analysis of token probability distributions (Figure 2) that offers some mechanistic insight into why the reweighting might help (deprioritizing low-information tokens like connectives).
The exploration of applying DFT in an offline RL/rejection-sampling setting and comparing it against DPO, RFT, PPO, and GRPO is a useful additional data point for practitioners.
weaknesses: Novelty is thin and largely overlaps with concurrent/contemporaneous work explicitly discussed in the paper itself (Qin & Springenberg 2025 iw-SFT, Wang et al. 2025, Du et al. 2025, Abdolmaleki et al. 2025), all of which already connect SFT to RL via implicit/importance reward weighting. The paper's differentiator -- multiplying the loss by the model's own token probability with a stop-gradient -- is a very small technical delta over these existing ideas, and the 'first to rigorously establish equivalence' claim is overstated given how close prior work already is.

The theoretical derivation (Eq. 5-6) relies on an importance-sampling identity that is only exact in expectation over infinitely many resampled trajectories matching y*; in practice only the single observed y* is used per example, so the 'resample+reweight' reinterpretation is more of a reformulation/intuition than a rigorous new result, and the claimed 'unbounded variance' argument is not empirically verified (e.g., no measurement of gradient variance across training).

Comparisons with the closest baseline (iw-SFT) are mixed and somewhat inconsistently framed: iw-SFT outperforms DFT on Qwen2.5-Math-7B in both the SFT setting (Table 2) and notably in the offline RL setting on several benchmarks (Table 3, e.g., AIME24, Olympiad Bench), yet the narrative selectively emphasizes DFT's wins and downplays or explains away these losses, which raises concerns about cherry-picking in the presentation.

Evaluation is confined entirely to mathematical reasoning tasks and models up to 7B parameters (explicitly acknowledged as a limitation), which is a narrow scope for claims about general SFT generalization; no code, instruction-following, or other NLP tasks are tested despite the generality of the claims made in the abstract/intro.

Only 1 training epoch is used and hyperparameters for SFT/DFT appear to follow 'recommended' settings without clear evidence that SFT baselines were comparably tuned; the hyperparameter ablation (Fig. 3) only sweeps 4 learning rates and 4 batch sizes on one model, which is insufficient to rule out that part of the SFT vs DFT gap stems from suboptimal SFT tuning.

No variance/error bars or statistical significance testing are reported despite using stochastic decoding (16 samples) on small benchmarks like AIME24 (30 problems) where differences of 1-2 points are within noise, undermining the certainty of several claimed 'significant' improvements.

The explanation in Section 4.3.1 relating DFT's bimodal token-probability effect to deprioritizing 'grammatical' tokens is qualitative/anecdotal (a few example words) rather than rigorously quantified, weakening the claimed mechanistic understanding.

Writing contains multiple typos/inconsistencies (e.g., 'focs' instead of 'focus', 'GPPO' instead of 'PPO', inconsistent indexing in Eq. 8 using t and y* without proper token definition), suggesting the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

The comparison claiming DFT surpasses online RL methods (GRPO/PPO) is based on a single model (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B) and a single data-generation setup, which is too narrow to support the strong generalization claim made in the abstract that this offers 'a practical alternative' to RL.

strengths: Provides a clear and intuitive theoretical framing that recasts the SFT gradient as a policy-gradient update with an implicit, inverse-probability-weighted reward, offering an explanation for SFT's poor generalization relative to RL.
The proposed fix (DFT) is extremely simple (reweighting the CE loss by the stop-gradient token probability), requiring only a one-line code change, which makes it highly practical and easy to adopt.

Extensive empirical validation across five different base models (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B, LLaMA-3.2-3B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, DeepSeekMath-7B) and five math reasoning benchmarks, showing consistent and often large improvements over standard SFT, including on benchmarks where SFT actually degrades performance (e.g., Olympiad Bench, AIME24).

Interesting additional experiments: convergence/sample-efficiency analysis (Figure 1), comparison against a concurrent and closely related method (iw-SFT), an offline-RL exploration where DFT is competitive with or exceeds GRPO/PPO/DPO/RFT, and a token-probability-distribution analysis that gives some mechanistic insight into why DFT differs from SFT.
Hyperparameter sensitivity ablations (learning rate, batch size) help rule out the possibility that the SFT baseline was simply under-tuned.
weaknesses: The claimed novelty of 'rigorously establishing' the SFT-RL gradient equivalence is somewhat overstated, since the paper itself cites multiple very recent concurrent works (Wang et al. 2025, Qin & Springenberg 2025, Du et al. 2025) that make essentially the same connection via reward/importance weighting; the derivation in Eqs. 5-6 (inserting an importance ratio against a Dirac-delta expert distribution) is also somewhat informal and not accompanied by a rigorous variance bound to support the 'unbounded variance' claim.

Comparisons to the closest concurrent baseline (iw-SFT) are mixed rather than uniformly favorable: iw-SFT outperforms DFT on Qwen2.5-Math-7B in both the SFT and offline-RL settings (and on several individual benchmarks such as AIME24 and Olympiad Bench), which weakens the claim of consistently superior generalization.

Evaluation is confined entirely to mathematical reasoning tasks; no results are shown for other domains (code, general instruction following, commonsense QA) or for larger models (13B+), as acknowledged in the Limitations, which limits confidence in the generality of the method.

The RL baseline comparisons (DPO, RFT, PPO, GRPO) use a different training-data construction pipeline (rejection sampling from the base model) than DFT/SFT, and hyperparameters for the RL baselines appear not to be extensively tuned, raising questions about whether the comparison to online/offline RL methods is fully apples-to-apples.
No training-run variance/seed analysis is reported (only inference-time averaging over 16 decoding runs), so it is unclear how stable the reported gains are to training stochasticity.

The polarizing/bimodal effect on token probabilities (favoring already-confident tokens, suppressing low-probability ones) could plausibly hurt output diversity or cause underfitting on rare-but-important tokens; this risk is noted qualitatively but not quantitatively analyzed (e.g., via entropy or downstream diversity metrics).

strengths: The paper proposes a genuinely simple, one-line modification to the SFT loss (multiplying by the stop-gradient token probability) that is trivial to implement and computationally free, making it highly practical.

Extensive empirical validation across many model families (LLaMA-3.2/3.1, Qwen2.5-Math, DeepSeekMath, Qwen2.5-Coder, Qwen2.5-VL) and scales (1.5B-8B), and across multiple domains (math reasoning, code generation, multi-modal reasoning), showing consistent and often large improvements over standard SFT.

Strong results on especially hard benchmarks (AIME24, OlympiadBench, AMC23) where standard SFT frequently underperforms or even degrades relative to the base model, while DFT reliably improves performance -- a meaningful and non-trivial finding.

Useful additional experiments: offline RL comparison against DPO/RFT/PPO/GRPO, PEFT/LoRA setting, hyperparameter (LR/batch size) sensitivity ablation, and a direct comparison against the concurrent iw-SFT method, which together strengthen confidence that the gains are not merely an artifact of poor SFT tuning.

The empirical analysis of post-training token probability distributions (Figure 2) provides an interesting qualitative story (polarization effect, deprioritizing function words) that helps explain the mechanism behind DFT's improved generalization.
Convergence/sample-efficiency analysis (Figure 1) adds useful evidence for practical benefits beyond final accuracy.
weaknesses: The core theoretical contribution -- casting SFT as policy gradient with an implicit Dirac-delta reward via importance sampling -- is a fairly standard algebraic manipulation and overlaps substantially with several concurrent/contemporaneous works cited in the paper (Du et al. 2025, Wang et al. 2025, Qin & Springenberg 2025/iw-SFT, Abdolmaleki et al. 2025), somewhat undercutting the claimed novelty of the 'RL perspective.'

The Appendix A.4 gradient analysis reveals that DFT's gradient reduces to simply ∇θ π(y*|x), i.e., directly maximizing raw probability instead of log-probability. This is a much simpler characterization than the RL/importance-sampling framing suggests, and the paper does not adequately justify why this particular exact cancellation (as opposed to other partial reweighting schemes) is the principled 'fix,' beyond intuition.

Direct comparison with the concurrent iw-SFT baseline (Table 5) is mixed: iw-SFT outperforms DFT on Qwen2.5-Math-7B by a non-trivial margin, weakening the claim of consistent superiority and highlighting that the proposed method is not decisively better than similar recently proposed reweighting approaches.

No variance/statistical significance analysis is reported for the main results despite using Average@16 evaluation, making it hard to assess whether reported gains (especially on small benchmarks like AIME24 with very few problems) are statistically robust.

The RL comparison (Table 2) is conducted only on a single model (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B), limiting generalizability of the claim that DFT is competitive with or superior to online RL methods like PPO/GRPO.

Some baseline SFT configurations appear to hurt performance relative to the base model (e.g., Qwen2.5-Math-7B on AIME24, Olympiad Bench), which is unusual and raises the possibility that the SFT baseline hyperparameters are suboptimal, inflating DFT's relative advantage; while an LR/batch-size ablation is provided, it does not fully rule out this concern (e.g., no exploration of different weight decay, epochs, or warm-up schedules for SFT).
Code is not yet released at submission/review time, limiting immediate reproducibility.

The theoretical claim that inverse-probability weighting is 'the' fundamental cause of SFT's poor generalization is argued qualitatively but not established rigorously (e.g., no formal generalization bound or convergence guarantee), leaving the causal story somewhat speculative.

strengths: The core idea (reweighting the SFT/CE loss by the model's own token probability, a one-line change) is simple and easy to implement.

Broad empirical coverage: multiple model families and scales (LLaMA, DeepSeekMath, Qwen2.5-Math/Coder/VL), multiple domains (math, code, multimodal reasoning), and an offline-RL comparison against DPO/RFT/PPO/GRPO.
Consistent qualitative trend across nearly all settings that DFT outperforms vanilla SFT, including on hard benchmarks (AIME24, OlympiadBench) where SFT sometimes degrades performance.
A reasonably extensive appendix with ablations (learning rate, batch size, LoRA/PEFT, alternate training data) and comparison to a concurrent method (iw-SFT).
An attempt at mechanistic analysis via token probability distributions (Figure 2) to explain why the reweighting might reduce overfitting on low-information tokens.
weaknesses: The central theoretical derivation (Eq. 5) that casts the SFT gradient as a policy-gradient with importance weight 1/πθ is essentially a tautological algebraic rewriting (multiply-and-divide by the model probability over a delta-function reward); it does not constitute a genuinely new on-policy estimator (sampling y from πθ and keeping only y=y* is degenerate/unusable in practice), so the 'RL perspective' framing is more rhetorical than substantive, and the appendix's own derivation (A.4) shows the final DFT gradient is simply −∇θπθ(y*|x), i.e. directly maximizing raw probability instead of log-probability — a much more mundane characterization than the elaborate RL narrative suggests.

The novelty relative to prior reweighted-CE/behavioral-cloning methods (GOLD, focal loss, MixCE, iw-SFT) is thin; the distinction drawn from these works (e.g., 'no unknown behavior policy needed') is somewhat overstated given the similarity of the final objective (p·log p).

Comparison with the concurrent method iw-SFT is mixed (iw-SFT outperforms DFT on Qwen2.5-Math-7B by a notable margin), undermining the claim of consistent superiority and suggesting the gains may be model/benchmark-dependent rather than a general property of the method.

No variance/seed information is reported anywhere; given small benchmark sizes (e.g., AIME24 has only 30 problems) and single training runs, many of the reported point differences could be within noise, yet are discussed as large, consistent effects.

The baseline SFT numbers look unusually weak in places (e.g., catastrophic collapse to 0.00 on AIME24 for LLaMA-3.2-3B/3.1-8B, and SFT hurting Olympiad/AMC23 scores), which inflates the apparent DFT advantage; it is unclear whether this reflects an intrinsic SFT flaw or simply an under-regularized/overtrained SFT baseline (e.g., too many epochs/steps without early stopping, as suggested by the declining SFT curves in Figure 1).

The claim that DFT (an offline, reward-free reweighting of a fixed expert dataset) matches or beats online RL methods (PPO, GRPO) is a strong claim that deserves more scrutiny; RL baselines use a possibly suboptimal fixed learning rate (1e-6) and the comparison setup (single run, no tuning sweep for RL baselines) raises concerns about fairness.
No code is released (link is a placeholder), limiting reproducibility despite claims of a 'simple one-line change.'

The explanation in Section 4.5 for why DFT helps (deprioritizing grammatical/connective tokens) is post-hoc and anecdotal rather than rigorously validated, weakening the paper's claim to be 'theoretically motivated.'

strengths: Provides a clean, well-motivated theoretical derivation connecting the SFT gradient to an on-policy policy gradient via importance sampling, identifying the implicit 1/π(y*) weighting as the source of instability.
The proposed fix (DFT) is extremely simple—a one-line change to the SFT loss—making it easy to adopt in existing training pipelines.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning five model families (LLaMA, Qwen2.5-Math, DeepSeekMath) and multiple scales, plus cross-domain validation on code generation (HumanEval, MultiPL-E) and multimodal reasoning (MathVerse, MathVision, WeMath).
Comparison against a concurrent method (iw-SFT) and additional ablations (PEFT/LoRA setting, learning rate and batch size sensitivity) add robustness to the empirical claims.

The offline RL experiments, where DFT is shown to be competitive with or exceed online methods like PPO and GRPO while requiring no reference model, is a practically interesting result if it holds up.

The token-probability distribution analysis (Figure 2) provides some interpretability into why the method behaves differently from vanilla SFT, with a plausible connection to deprioritizing low-information tokens.
weaknesses: The core theoretical contribution—casting SFT as RL with an implicit reward and reweighting by probability—is closely related to several contemporaneous works cited in the related work section (Wang et al. 2025, Qin & Springenberg 2025, GOLD/Pang & He 2021), limiting the novelty of the framing itself; the main new element is largely the token-level 'sg(π)' weighting choice.

Appendix A.4 shows that the DFT gradient reduces to directly maximizing πθ(y*|x) (i.e., -∇θπθ rather than -∇θ log πθ), which means the method is essentially equivalent to a known alternative loss (probability-matching rather than log-likelihood maximization); this simpler characterization is not discussed in the main text, and the 'RL perspective' framing, while elegant, may be more of a narrative device than a necessary theoretical insight.

Some reported gains are surprisingly large (e.g., SFT with DFT nearly doubling Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B's accuracy on AMC23, and DFT outperforming fully tuned PPO/GRPO), which is inconsistent with the common finding that naive SFT on CoT data typically degrades already RL-tuned math models; this raises questions about whether baselines (especially PPO/GRPO with only a single fixed low learning rate and no apparent extensive tuning) were adequately tuned for fair comparison.
No variance/confidence intervals are reported despite small test sets (e.g., AIME24 has only 30 problems), making it hard to assess statistical significance of fractional-point differences.

The explanation for why downweighting low-probability tokens helps (stopwords/connectives) is anecdotal and not rigorously validated; it is plausible that some low-probability tokens are actually important rare but semantically critical tokens (e.g., specific numbers or operators in math reasoning), which the method may inadvertently suppress.

Table 5 shows the concurrent method iw-SFT outperforms DFT by a non-trivial margin on Qwen2.5-Math-7B, which is downplayed in the discussion; a more balanced analysis of when/why DFT underperforms would strengthen the paper.
Code is not yet released ('will be available'), and the largest model tested is 8B, leaving open how the method scales to larger, more capable LLMs.

Baseline/offline-RL comparisons (DPO, RFT, PPO, GRPO) use different frameworks (ms-swift vs verl) and different learning rates without extensive tuning details, raising concerns about comparison fairness.
